newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania presidency still in Constantinescu's grasp.
newsitem.headline: Romania presidency still in Constantinescu's grasp.

text.p: Emil Constantinescu, still hopeful of unseating Romanian President Ion Iliescu, is a mild-mannered geology professor who took to the streets to demonstrate against communist rule.

Constantinescu trailed Iliescu by three points in Sunday's first round vote, though his centrist Democratic Convention scored a major victory in parliamentary polls and should form Romania's first non-communist government of the modern era.
Constantinesu's supporters are still convinced he will score a major upset and win the November 17 run-off round.
A former rector of Bucharest University, he was drafted into the political front line by the Convention (CDR) because of his untarnished reputation.
"There are no dark corners in my life and consequently I cannot be blackmailed," Constantinescu repeated throughout the two-month campaign. "Nobody can put pressure on me."
Constantinescu, 56, became CDR leader in 1992, the year he was beaten by Iliescu in his first run at the presidency.

This time his performance has been more polished. His calm manner contrasted sharply with Iliescu's reputation as a shrewd ex-communist career politician. Few have doubted Constantinescu's commitment or sincerity.
"Campaigning in the remotest villages, I understood one thing - Romania is in deep crisis," he said after the first exit polls as he greeted cheering students from atop a car.
His party campaign was based on a "Contract with Romania." He pledged to step down in 200 days if he failed to cut taxes, improve living standards and modernise decaying industries.
That meant tearing the entire post-communist system down -- and getting rid of its president.

"Re-electing Iliescu would spell catastrophe for Romania," he said during the campaign. "His people have led the country and pillaged the national wealth. People know this and they know that they have been robbed."
Iliescu's camp accused him of wanting to bring back Romania's exiled King Michael. But the charge did not stick.

Slim and impeccably groomed with a beard, Constantinescu was a died-in-the-wool anti-Communist and one of the few teachers who joined students in December 1989 street protests that led to the overthrow of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Six months later he took part in an anti-government rally broken up by left-wing miners who sacked central Bucharest.
He has said he will reject the trappings of public office if elected and refuse to live in the vast presidential palace.
"I'll move into a villa with my family. I will go for a walk in the evenings and talk to the neighbours," he said.

Constantinescu was born in Tighina - now called Bendery, an ethnic flashpoint between Romanian-speakers and Slavs in the former Soviet republic of Moldova. He is married and has two children -- both students.
